papers.title: Decoding Clade-Specific bNAb-HIV-1 Env Interactions Using Machine Learning
papers.abstract: Human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) exhibits extensive genetic diversity, posing a major challenge to AIDS vaccine development. Broadly neutralizing antibodies (bNAbs) isolated from HIV-1-infected individuals offer valuable templates for designing broadly protective immunogens. Here, structural and energetic descriptors extracted from experimentally resolved bNAb/HIV-1 Envelope (Env) protein-protein complexes were used to develop machine-learning (ML) models predicting binding free energies ({triangleup}G) and dissociation constants (KD) across multiple HIV-1 clades. Among the algorithms evaluated, extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost) achieved the best predictive performance, with training and test R2 values of 0.92 and 0.658, respectively. Applying the optimized model to HIV-1 datasets revealed clade-dependent binding patterns, with clade B showing the greatest variability and clade G exhibiting signatures associated with reduced neutralization potency. Predicted {triangleup}G of different bNAb classes followed the trend gp120-gp41 interface {approx} fusion domain > CD4 binding site (CD4bs) > V1V2 loop {approx} V3-glycan, consistent with experimentally reported affinity profiles of benchmark bNAbs. Clade C exhibited intermediate {triangleup}G with PGT121, VRC01, and 10-1074 maintaining high-affinity interactions, whereas PG9 and 2G12 show reduced binding affinity. These findings offer quantitative insight into clade-specific bNAb binding energetics and demonstrate the potential of machine-learning approaches to guide HIV-1 immunogen design and vaccine development.

papers.title: Identification and targeting of a novel drug pocket in the tumour angiogenesis regulator RhoJ
papers.abstract: The Rho GTPase RhoJ is a key regulator of tumour angiogenesis and has been identified as a target for anti-angiogenic drug design. Its high sequence conservation with the related Rho GTPase Cdc42 complicates selective drug discovery. RhoJ has a unique N-terminal extension (Asn2-Lys19) that is absent in Cdc42 and other Rho GTPases. Here, we use molecular dynamics simulations to identify a novel allosteric pocket formed by the RhoJ N-terminus and show that this pocket contributes to interactions with key downstream signalling partners. Structure-based virtual screening of small molecules targeting this pocket identified the antifungal terconazole as a potential binder. Computational docking revealed that terconazole occupies the N-terminal pocket, sharing critical contacts with the interface between RhoJ and PAK3, a key interacting partner. To validate this, we developed an optimized bioluminescence resonance energy transfer (eBRET2)-based biosensor to monitor the interaction between RhoJ and PAK3 in live cells and saw that terconazole disrupted the RhoJ:PAK3 interaction in a dose-dependent manner. Together, our MD results show that the RhoJ N-terminal extension assumes structure on binding to PAK3 and contributes to that interaction, while our cellular biosensor data support targeting this pocket to modulate the RhoJ:PAK3 interaction. The ability of terconazole to bind to the N-terminal pocket and disrupt PAK3 binding provides proof of concept for the specific targeting of RhoJ in the development of novel anti-angiogenic drugs.

papers.title: Engineering potent avian GPR25 agonists using an ostrich CXCL17 gene relic
papers.abstract: C-X-C motif chemokine ligand 17 (CXCL17) activates G protein-coupled receptor 25 (GPR25) in most vertebrate lineages. Although birds appear to have lost functional CXCL17, CXCL17 gene relics and intact GPR25 genes persist in certain taxa. This study investigated whether a fragment encoded by an avian CXCL17 gene relic could guide the engineering of potent agonists for avian GPR25s. A 22-residue C-terminal fragment encoded by African ostrich CXCL17 gene relic was grafted onto the corresponding position of loggerhead turtle or human CXCL17, and the resulting hybrids were prepared via bacterial overexpression and functionally characterized via cell-based assays. The turtle-ostrich and human-ostrich CXCL17 hybrids showed no detectable activity at turtle or human GPR25 but exhibited substantially greater potency than their parental proteins at two avian GPR25s in {beta}-arrestin recruitment assays, with half-maximal effective concentrations of approximately 25 and 100 nM at the ostrich receptor and 5 and 13 nM at the mallard receptor, respectively. Both hybrids bound directly to the ostrich or mallard GPR25 in homogenous ligand-receptor binding assays and induced migration of transfected cells expressing the ostrich or mallard receptor in chemotaxis assays. These findings demonstrate that a fragment encoded by the ostrich CXCL17 gene relic confers potent avian GPR25 agonism and establishes the C-terminus as the primary driver of species selectivity. These hybrids provide functional surrogate tools for probing avian GPR25 biology.

papers.title: Allosteric covalent inhibition of cereblon through cryptic cysteine targeting
papers.abstract: Thalidomide-derived cereblon (CRBN) modulators are among the most clinically impactful targeted protein degradation therapeutics, redirecting the CRL4-CRBN E3 ubiquitin ligase to degrade disease-driving neosubstrates. All current CRBN-targeting IMiDs and CELMoDs engage a single orthosteric pocket, leaving CRBN's conformational landscape largely unexploited pharmacologically. Using cysteine-directed chemoproteomic screening, we identified covalent ligands that engage Cys287, a cryptic allosteric pocket distal to the orthosteric site. Our lead compound, VVD-105917, acts as a pan-inhibitor of IMiD/CELMoD-driven neosubstrate degradation. Cryo-EM structures reveal that covalent Cys287 engagement traps CRBN in its open, inactive conformation, resolving a previously unobserved N-terminal segment and sensor loop. Sequential incubation experiments show the conformational outcome depends on ligand addition order, demonstrating that even potent CELMoD-driven closure can be overridden by allosteric engagement. A recently reported ligand at this same pocket produces the opposite effect, promoting rather than blocking closure, indicating the Cys287 site is mechanistically sign-switchable. These findings establish covalent chemoproteomics as a strategy for discovering and controlling E3 ligase conformational switches.

papers.title: P4HA1 and P4HA2 accept both shared and isoenzyme-specific substrate residues in type I collagen to directly and indirectly orchestrate its post-translational modification landscape
papers.abstract: Type I collagen, the most abundant protein of vertebrate organisms, is polymerized into a macroscopic-scale fibrillar network, the detailed arrangement of which is controlled by numerous post-translational modifications (PTMs) to determine the biomechanics of connective tissues. Its most frequent post-translational modification, prolyl-4-hydroxylation (P4H), catalyzed by prolyl-4-hydroxylases (P4HAs), occupies about 100 residue positions per procollagen alpha chain and is crucial to stabilize its triple helical building block thermodynamically. Recently, the two main P4HAs, P4HA1 and P4HA2, were found to exhibit mutual substrate specificity based on the nature of the amino acid residue standing N-terminally to the considered substrate residue. Independently, the activities of both enzymes were suggested to influence lysyl residue hydroxylation and glycosylation. To clarify these findings, we performed here a proteome-, tripeptide- and amino acid-scale analysis of prolyl and lysyl modifications of collagens, both in the established ATDC5 cell line and in primary mouse skin fibroblasts after adenovirus-mediated Crispr/Cas9 invalidation of either or both P4ha1 and/or P4ha2 genes. We conclude that both enzymes have no more than 18 and 14 respective specific substrate positions among more than 200 potential P4H sites available on type I collagen alpha chains. Combining procollagen tryptic peptide and tripeptide analysis, we confirm that glutamate localized N-terminally to potential P4H sites determines the substrate specificity of P4HA2. P4HA1-specific sites are instead preceded by phenylalanine, lysine, arginine, asparagine or histidine. Furthermore, we evidence that P4H is not required for prolyl-3-hydroxylation at the so-called A1 site and demonstrate that it reduces lysyl glycosylation at multiple sites in a cell-type-dependent manner. These findings highlight the strategic molecular function of P4HA1 and P4HA2 within the collagen maturation machinery, for, together, steering subtle collagen post-translational modifications.

papers.title: Benchmarking the Performance of a Commercial Electrostatic Linear Ion Trap (ELIT) Charge Detection Mass Spectrometer For Higher-Order Antibody Aggregate Analysis
papers.abstract: Higher-order antibody aggregates remain challenging to characterize using conventional mass spectrometry because of their low abundance, broad mass distributions, and extensive heterogeneity. Here, the practical performance of a commercial electrostatic linear ion trap charge detection mass spectrometer (XevoTM CDMS) was evaluated for therapeutic antibody analysis. The platform provided reproducible mass and charge measurements, with repeatability and intermediate-precision RSDs below 1%, and maintained consistent mass determination across the concentration and solution conditions examined. Controlled mixtures of antibody-derived species showed a linear molar-ratio-dependent ion response, supporting semi-quantitative estimation of relative species abundance under defined conditions. For heat-stressed trastuzumab, CDMS measurements were qualitatively consistent with SEC-MALS, mass photometry, and conventional native MS, while enabling direct mass determination of individual ions within highly heterogeneous high-molecular-weight (HMW) populations that exhibited extensive charge-state overlap and could not be reliably deconvoluted by conventional native MS. High-duty-cycle acquisition increased sampling of low-abundance, high-m/z ions and improved access to higher-order aggregate signals. Joint single ion mass-charge analysis further differentiated statistical ion families within the broad HMW fraction and related major mass differences to independently obtained compositional information. These results support commercial XevoTM CDMS as a practical multidimensional platform for antibody aggregate characterization.

papers.title: A potent macrocyclic peptide binder enables effector-free crystallization of the GTPase RAB27A
papers.abstract: RAB27A is a member of a highly conserved family of small GTPases that regulate intracellular vesicle trafficking. Multiple studies have linked RAB27A cellular activity to exosome-mediated modulation of the tumour microenvironment and inflammatory signalling, highlighting it as an attractive target for drug discovery. However, identifying structurally validated and selective inhibitors of the RAB27A-effector interaction has proven challenging, partly because wild-type RAB27A crystallizes only in complex with effector proteins such as Slp2a. Using mRNA display, we identified macrocyclic peptide ligands that target the RAB27A effector-binding interface. Optimisation of initial hits led to IMP2660, a nanomolar-affinity RAB27A binder that effectively disrupts RAB27A-effector interactions. IMP2660 enabled determination of a 2.1[A] structure of active-state RAB27A bound to a noncovalent macrocyclic peptide in the absence of an effector, revealing structural features of the effector-binding surface and providing a platform for future structure-guided ligand development.

papers.title: Rational Design of a Photoactivated Fluorescent Probe for Thiol-ene Mediated Protein Labelling
papers.abstract: Fluorescent labelling of biomolecules enables the visualization and tracking of molecular processes in cells, providing insights into cellular function and disease mechanisms. Despite recent advances in bioorthogonal labelling, efficient and site-selective strategies for targeting alkene functionalities remain limited. Here, we report AbzSH, a compact aminobenzamide-based fluorescent thiol probe for selective alkene labelling through thiol-ene ligation. Photoinduced ligation proceeds under mild, radical-mediated conditions in aqueous media and exhibits broad substrate compatibility, including carbohydrate, amino acid, and steroid scaffolds. The method is readily extended to protein labelling, enabling selective modification of both chemically functionalized proteins and engineered proteins containing genetically encoded alkene motifs. Efficient and chemoselective labelling was further demonstrated in complex cell lysates, highlighting the robustness of the approach in biologically relevant environments. Collectively, these results establish AbzSH as a versatile fluorescent probe for alkene-directed biomolecular labelling and provide a broadly applicable platform for chemical biology, molecular imaging, proteomics, and drug discovery.

papers.title: Identification of Cysteine-Reactive Early Mitotic Inhibitors
papers.abstract: Cancer remains a pervasive health problem for millions of Americans, and defining effective anticancer therapeutics remains a major obstacle to the long-term survival of patients. Recent advances in novel chemistries and chemical libraries have enabled researchers to discover and develop covalent inhibitors to treat various diseases, including cancer. This has spurred the generation of cysteine-targeting covalent compound libraries that have not been fully explored within the context of the cell cycle and cell division, which are attractive targets for inhibiting cancer proliferation. We report a novel, cell-based high-content chemical screening strategy for discovering early mitotic spindle assembly inhibitors. We coupled this strategy with a cysteine-reactive covalent compound library containing 3,520 molecules to identify novel early mitotic inhibitors. These inhibitors included a microtubule depolymerizer, a mitotic spindle positioning disruptor, and compounds affecting mitotic spindle structure and chromosome alignment. Two of these compounds triggered mitotic arrest and reduced cell viability at nanomolar concentrations. These inhibitors serve as chemical probes to investigate mechanisms of early cell division and to develop novel cancer therapeutics.

papers.title: Unfolding of the disease-linked bank vole prion protein E200K in the context of PrPSc propagation
papers.abstract: The elucidation of the atomistic structure of PrPSc has, disappointingly, not revealed the mechanism underlying prion propagation. This is because PrPSc has been shown to be a standard amyloid, and as such, it can only template a polypeptide chain that is unfolded. Therefore, while PrPSc can easily template the disordered ~90-120 domain of an incoming PrPC molecule, it does not have any obvious capacity to template its ~121-231 folded domain (FD). The FD needs to accommodate into the ~121-230 PrPSc surface, an inert "Procrustean bed". We have recently proposed that unfolding of the FD is a prerequisite for its conversion to the PrPSc conformation and using experimental and computational methods identified the likely early events of such process using bank vole (BV)PrP(90-231) as our working model. We concluded that a key early event is the destabilization of the short {beta}1-{beta}2 assembly, and that the segment contiguous to the disordered tail, ~121-140, encompassing {beta}1 and its adjacent coils, is the most likely region to unfold first. In the present study we applied the same methodology to the disease-related PrP mutant E200K. E200K is the most prevalent mutation leading to familial prion disease in humans, yet the stability of its FD is only marginally lower compared to that of the protein with the wild type (wt) sequence. We, therefore, aimed at assessing whether the early unfolding events of BVPrPC(E200K) are similar or different to those of wtBVPrPC and whether such early unfolding route might provide insight into the extreme capacity of PrPC(E200K) to spontaneously generate PrPSc. It should be noted that generation and propagation of PrPSc are distinct phenomena, even though both are mechanistically related and dependent on conformational changes in PrPC. Our data show that early unfolding events of BVPrPC(E200K) are essentially similar to those of wt BVPrPC. However, interesting nuances exist.

papers.title: Myopathy-causing variants of PYROXD1 converge on impaired RNA ligation
papers.abstract: RNA ligation is critical for RNA processing pathways including pre-tRNA splicing. RTCB is the only essential RNA ligase in humans and the catalytic subunit of the tRNA ligase complex (tRNA-LC). Its active site is sensitive to oxidation and strictly depends on oxidoreductase PYROXD1, the only tRNA-LC subunit with multiple known pathogenic protein-coding variants. The role of RNA ligation in PYROXD1 myopathy remained contentious: loss of PYROXD1 primarily affects mitochondria, and ligation-linked readouts are inconsistent in existing assays. Here, we reveal that PYROXD1 is physically, genetically and functionally committed to the tRNA-LC. Selectively impairing RTCB activation reproduces hallmarks of PYROXD1 dysfunction, including mitochondrial deregulation. Using degron-based depletion of endogenous PYROXD1, we show that all six single amino acid variants reported in patients fail to sustain RNA ligation in proportion to their clinical severity. The variants segregate into three mechanistic classes: they lower protein stability, disrupt the NADPH-mediated conformational switch, or impair RTCB engagement by the C-terminal tail, a sequence unique to PYROXD1 and directly affected in the most severe variant D500N. Variant-level measurements in the degron model predict outcomes in homozygous and compound heterozygous patient fibroblasts. Together, these data establish impaired RNA ligation as the driver of PYROXD1 pathogenicity.

papers.title: A KaiA Conformational Switch Links Day-Night Transitions to Clock Robustness
papers.abstract: Biological clocks require mechanisms that enable transition between temporal phases and buffer against environmental fluctuations. In the cyanobacterial KaiABC-based circadian oscillator, KaiA has been regarded as a daytime activator that is passively sequestered at night. Here we define KaiA as a conformationally regulated activator and an active catalyst of the night-to-dawn transition. We identify a single linker helix, 5, that acts as a structural switch, mediating a domain-driven "tug-of-war" that sets the open-closed equilibrium in KaiA. Structure-guided mutations that shift this balance in either direction abolish stable rhythmicity both in vitro and in cells. Also, we show that substoichiometric KaiA dismantles nighttime KaiB-KaiC complexes through interactions with the KaiC C-terminal tails and likely initiates an autocatalytic feedback loop that resets the phosphorylation cycle at dawn. Furthermore, we present two independent kinetic models that offer distinct, deterministic explanations for the clock's low-temperature amplitude decline and failure at 20 {degrees} C.

papers.title: Molecular Insights into the Collagen-binding Specificity of Discoidin Domain Receptors
papers.abstract: Discoidin domain receptors, DDR1 and DDR2, are a subfamily of homologous receptor tyrosine kinases that are activated by the extracellular matrix (ECM) collagens. Together the two DDRs recognize at least seven of the twenty-eight known collagen types (Col1-28) with distinct specificities. For example, Col1-3 and Col5 that exist as fibres in connective tissues activate both DDRs whereas Col6 microfilaments found in ECM of skeletal muscles preferentially activates DDR1. Further, Col4 found in basement membrane as mesh-like networks preferentially activates DDR1 but similarly network-forming Col10 abundant in cartilage preferentially binds and activates DDR2. These preferential interactions activate specific signalling pathways driving distinct physiological processes and pathologies, yet their molecular basis is currently not understood. Here, we show that the collagen-binding specificity of the DDRs is determined by electrostatic interactions at the receptor-ligand binding interface. The collagen-binding site in the two DDRs differ in the nature and placement of electrostatically charged residues. The known DDR-binding epitopes in Col1-Col3 also contain charged residues positioned to interact with those on the DDRs. We hypothesize that these interfacial electrostatic interactions between the DDRs and collagens guide their recognition specificity. We experimentally test this hypothesis and show that triple-helical peptides (THPs) containing rationally placed charged residues have biased affinities for the two DDRs. Aside from advancing mechanistic understanding of the different collagen-DDR interactions, our results can facilitate better understanding of the associated signalling pathways and the design of therapeutically active DDR-specific antagonists.

papers.title: Structural Basis for Angiotensin II Type I Receptor G Protein-biased Signaling
papers.abstract: Biased agonism at the angiotensin II type 1 receptor (AT1R) offers a promising strategy for developing safer cardiovascular therapeutics. While beta-arrestin-biased agonism has been extensively investigated, G protein-biased signaling remains poorly understood. Here, we report structures of AT1R coupled to G protein and either the endogenous agonist angiotensin II (AngII) or the G protein-biased agonist TRV055. The ligands adopt similar overall poses, with coordinated rearrangements extending from the orthosteric pocket to the intracellular surface. The structures provide a detailed view of a TM7-centered microswitch network linking ligand recognition to G protein coupling. Functional analyses of peptide analogs identify the ligand's amino terminus as a key determinant of G protein bias, while mutagenesis of the microswitch network shifts AngII toward beta-arrestin-biased signaling and converts the G protein-biased agonist TRV055 into a beta-arrestin-biased ligand. These findings establish a framework for G protein-biased AT1R activation and provide mechanistic insight for the rational design of pathway-selective GPCR therapeutics.

papers.title: Chemical foundation models reveal molecular principles underlying glycobiology
papers.abstract: Glycans encode biological specificity through branching, linkage and stereochemical diversity, and have traditionally been modelled using specialised computational representations distinct from those developed for general chemistry. It remains unclear to what extent representations learned from general molecular chemistry capture the molecular principles of glycobiology. Here, we systematically evaluate the transfer of chemical foundation models to glycobiology using standardized benchmarks spanning taxonomy, immunogenicity, glycosylation type and protein-glycan interactions. We show that atom-level representations learned from general chemistry encode biologically meaningful molecular organization, providing particularly strong performance for molecular recognition, including immunogenicity and protein-glycan interaction prediction. Fine-tuning reorganizes these representations into latent spaces aligned with glycan architecture, glycosylation programmes and molecular recognition. Mechanistic analyses identify stereochemistry as an important determinant of successful transfer, while tokenization, context length and conformer generation influence the representation of large, branched glycans. These representations generalize from natural glycans to synthetic glycomimetics and recover experimentally validated stereochemistry-dependent glycan-lectin recognition. Together, our findings demonstrate that molecular principles learned from general chemistry are sufficient to capture fundamental features of glycobiology. They position glycans as a specialised region of chemical space and chemical foundation models as a broadly applicable framework for glycan function prediction, molecular recognition and glycomimetic discovery.

papers.title: Affinity maturation of a single-domain antibody via rational mutagenesis informed by artificial intelligence
papers.abstract: Antibodies can originate from various sources such as animal immunizations, patient material, DNA/RNA libraries and (AI-based) de novo design. Pre-made (e.g. synthetic) DNA libraries have substantial advantages over traditional immunization campaigns in terms of speed, cost, animal welfare, amount of required antigen and the possibility to select against otherwise problematic (e.g. toxic, unstable or expensive) antigens. The main downside is that selections from these non-immune libraries often result in binders with relatively low affinity due to the absence of in vivo affinity maturation. Now that in silico structure prediction tools are coming of age, the resulting models could conceivably be used to rationally design mutations, e.g. to enhance binding affinity. Here we used a synthetic single-domain antibody (sdAb) library to select new binders against interleukin-12 (IL-12). One of the selected candidates, 2F3, was predicted to bind to the p40 subunit of IL-12 in a manner that would compete with binding of the receptor protein IL-12R{beta}1. Intriguingly, this epitope is also targeted by the clinically approved antibodies Briakinumab and Ustekinumab, which are used to treat a variety of inflammation disorders. The predicted structure of the IL-12/sdAb complex was used to rationally design eleven point mutations, of which three showed to enhance the binding affinity. By combining these mutations, we could enhance the affinity by eightfold compared to the original lead clone. This shows that correctly (AI-)predicted protein structural models can be used for rational mutagenesis to enhance binding affinity to relevant drug targets.

papers.title: Computational redesign of Chlamydomonas reinhardtii photosynthetic fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase from the Calvin-Benson-Bassham cycle improves both stability and catalytic capacities in vitro
papers.abstract: Photosynthetic carbon fixation is catalyzed by 11 enzymes in the Calvin-Benson-Bassham cycle, a highly conserved metabolic pathway in the green lineage. Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase (FBPase) contributes to the regeneration of the substrate of carboxylation. While non-photosynthetic paralogs of FBPases contribute to cytosolic neoglucogenesis in a well-documented manner, chloroplast FBPases specific regulations by phospho- and redox-posttranslational modifications, pH, cofactor binding, and homo-oligomeric exchange is only partially understood. In particular, FBPases from green microalgae are potentially target of a multiplicity of disulfide/dithiol exchanges that appear more complex than all their cytosolic and chloroplastic land-plant or cyanobacterial paralogs. In an attempt to decipher the molecular basis of chloroplast FBPase activities and precise redox regulations, we applied computational tools to extensively redesign its protein coding sequence, testing the simultaneous substitution of >13% of its amino acids as guided by distant homology. Resulting modified proteins in pure recombinant form were significantly more stable than the wild-type starting point, that was prone to denaturation or aggregation. In particular, redesigned FBPase favored the catalytically competent homo-tetrameric state. Thermal denaturation assays revealed that the redesign of FBPase sequence starkly increased in thermostability, in good correlation with an augmented enzymatic activity over long periods of time. By comparison with its wild-type counterpart, computationally redesigned FBPase allowed an extensive structure-function study that uncovered the multiplicity of redox regulations of microalgal paralog, their combined contribution to the assembly of the catalytically competent homo-tetrameric state, and will further facilitate molecular engineering of photosynthesis.

papers.title: To Recover or Not to Recover: A Urinary Proteomic Perspective on Severe Acute Kidney Injury
papers.abstract: Rationale & Objective Early prediction of renal non-recovery after acute kidney injury (AKI) could support risk-adapted follow-up and clinical decision-making. We evaluated whether a urinary fatty acid-binding protein 3 (FABP3)/apolipoprotein A-I (APOA1) ratio based on Total Protein Approach (TPA) quantification could discriminate renal recovery from non-recovery after severe AKI. Study Design Exploratory biomarker discovery study with outcome-blinded independent validation. Setting & Participants Critically ill adults with KDIGO stage 2 or 3 AKI. Urine was collected 48 hours after AKI diagnosis. The discovery cohort included 20 patients (10 recovered and 10 non-recovered), and the outcome-blinded validation cohort included 10 patients. New Predictor Urinary TPA-derived FABP3/APOA1 ratio (AKI^TPA index). Outcome Renal recovery at day 14, defined as survival with serum creatinine returning to within 0.3 mg/dL or 150% of baseline; patients not meeting these criteria were classified as having non-recovery. Analytical Approach Urinary proteins were analyzed by LC-MS/MS and quantified using TPA. Differential analysis identified FABP3 and APOA1 as oppositely associated with renal outcome. A predefined FABP3/APOA1 threshold of 1 classified patients as non-recovery-like (>1) or recovery-like (<1) and was subsequently applied to the outcome-blinded validation cohort. Results In the discovery cohort, the AKI^TPA index correctly classified 17 of 20 patients (accuracy, 85.0%; sensitivity, 80.0%; specificity, 90.0%; ROC AUC, 0.930). In the validation cohort, 9 patients were evaluable, of whom 7 were correctly classified (accuracy, 77.8%; sensitivity, 75.0%; specificity, 80.0%; ROC AUC, 0.950). Limitations The exploratory design and limited cohort size warrant further validation in larger, independent populations. Conclusions The urinary FABP3/APOA1 TPA ratio showed encouraging preliminary discrimination of renal recovery after severe AKI and warrants prospective clinical validation in larger, independent multicenter cohorts.

papers.title: Rapid, reversible RNA/DNA precipitation using rare earth ion coordination
papers.abstract: Efficient recovery and removal of nucleic acids remain major challenges in molecular biology, diagnostics, and viral-vector manufacturing. Conventional precipitation methods often require organic solvents, low temperatures, and extended centrifugation, while nuclease-based contaminant removal can be incomplete and/or is incompatible with downstream workflows. Here, we evaluate NADA, a trivalent rare earth-based reagent, for rapid, solvent-free precipitation of RNA and DNA, and ALGO-mediated recovery of the full range of properties of unmodified RNA. Using hepatitis B virus pre-genomic RNA, lambda bacteriophage DNA, and the HBV nucleocapsid as model systems, we show that NADA rapidly sequesters both ssRNA and dsDNA from solution, reducing Midori Green nucleic acid fluorescence and UV absorption to baseline levels. The NADA complex prevents HBV core protein binding to the HBV pgRNA, and therefore triggering of nucleocapsid formation, even when added simultaneously with core protein, suggesting that lanthanide ion coordination, out-competes the cognate Cp for viral RNA-binding interactions. Recovery with ALGO restores pgRNA integrity and functionality, enabling subsequent assembly of the expected T=4/T=3 nucleocapsids. In contrast, pre-assembled nucleocapsids resist NADA-ALGO treatment, demonstrating coat protein capsid-mediated protection of encapsidated pgRNA. Similar outcomes for lambda dsDNA establish NADA/ALGO as a rapid, reversible, and selective alternative platform for nucleic acid precipitation, with potential applications in viral particle purification, contaminant removal, and RNA handling workflows.

papers.title: Molecular mechanism of Aurora-A binding and activation by hnRNPK
papers.abstract: Aurora-A kinase (AurA) is a serine/threonine kinase regulated by protein binding partners such as TPX2, which interacts with the Y-pocket of the kinase domain. Although the canonical functions of AurA are mitotic, where it phosphorylates spindle-associated proteins such as TACC3, there is evidence for non-mitotic, chromatin-associated roles. Heterogenous nuclear ribonucleoprotein K (hnRNPK) is a transcriptional regulator and an AurA substrate, how AurA is activated in this pathway is unknown. Their interaction contributes to cancer-associated nuclear accumulation of AurA and has been implicated in driving oncogenic transcription of MYC. Here, we show that hnRNPK promotes AurA autophosphorylation and stimulates AurA activity. The interface was mapped to residues 330-380, an intrinsically disordered region of hnRNPK, and the AurA Y-pocket, using NMR spectroscopy and competitive-binding experiments with mitotic and synthetic AurA-binding partners. AlphaFold3 modelling of the complex predicted Phe339 and Trp345 at the kinase Y-pocket, and site-specific mutagenesis confirmed these as key residues for AurA binding and activation. Our work provides a mechanistic basis for hnRNPK-dependent activation of AurA and efficient phosphorylation of hnRNPK Ser379. Defining the AurA/hnRNPK interface highlights the Y-pocket as a target site for modulation of nuclear AurA, a potentially cancer-specific role of the kinase.

papers.title: Quantifying RNA Folding Equilibria from Unclassified Cryo-EM Particle Images
papers.abstract: Functional RNA structures are typically far more dynamic than most proteins solved by cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM). Flexible junctions and weak tertiary contacts produce broad conformational ensembles, and cryo-EM particle classification analyses discard unaligned particles, which inherently contain the information needed to quantify such broad ensembles. Here, we infer compositional and conformational distributions from unclassified particle images by Bayesian ensemble reweighting. We tested our approach on the P4-P6 domain of the Tetrahymena thermophila group I intron, a classic model system of Mg2+-dependent RNA folding. While stable monomeric and dimeric states yielded high-resolution reconstructions, analyses of abundant, flexible conformations required Bayesian ensemble inference. Our approach quantitatively captured the Mg2+-dependent folding transition, indicating that cryo-EM can report the abundance of coexisting RNA states in agreement with bulk solution measurements. These results showcase how quantitative studies of RNA folding can be achieved by combining cryo-EM measurements with statistical ensemble-inference tools.

papers.title: Decoupling of CO2 and O2 fluxes reveals oxygen-independent decarboxylation in anoxic mammalian cells
papers.abstract: Canonical understanding of cellular respiration holds that CO2 production tracks oxygen consumption, and mammalian cells deprived of oxygen are thought to rely on lactate fermentation, which yields no net CO2. Because standard respirometry infers CO2 flux either from oxygen consumption or from extracellular acidification rather than measuring it directly, a CO2 flux decoupled from oxygen would go undetected or be misattributed to glycolysis. Using direct measurement of CO2 and O2 fluxes from the gas phase in anoxic mammalian cells, we show that a substantial CO2 efflux persists after oxygen is fully removed. This anoxic flux scales linearly with normoxic CO2 and with cell mass, and exhibits a lower activation energy than normoxic respiration, suggesting a distinct rate-limiting chemistry. Pyruvate and -ketobutyrate increased the anoxic CO2 flux while lactate dehydrogenase inhibition abolished the pyruvate-induced increase, supporting a role for cytosolic NAD+ regeneration in oxygen-independent decarboxylation. 13C tracing identified a substantial glutamine-derived component, consistent with mitochondrial decarboxylation, and a smaller glucose-derived component associated with the cytosolic pentose phosphate pathway. Direct CO2 measurement thus reframes lactate dehydrogenase as an enabler of oxygen-independent decarboxylation.

papers.title: Cooperative IDR-folded domain interplay governs HP1α phase separation and underlies biphasic regulation by pathogenic poly-PR
papers.abstract: HP1 undergoes liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS), yet the prevailing model, which attributes condensation almost entirely to intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), leaves the role of its folded domains unresolved. Using solution and solid-state NMR, we show that HP1 LLPS is instead governed by reciprocal interplay between IDRs and folded domains. Within the condensed phase, solid-state NMR reveals a dynamic hierarchy: the chromoshadow domain (CSD) assembles into polymorphic oligomers that form rigid cores, while the phosphorylation sites on the N-terminal extension (NTE) remain highly mobile, challenging their proposed role as stable multivalent hubs. Phosphorylation of the NTE instead promotes LLPS primarily by increasing local rigidity and releasing the NTE from the chromodomain (CD) to relieve autoinhibition, with electrostatic charge contributing secondarily. The C-terminal extension (CTE) suppresses phase separation through two routes: weakening the association between the hinge region (HR) and the CSD, and inhibiting interactions between CSD dimers. ALS-associated poly-PR targets this network at the NTE and exerts concentration-dependent biphasic regulation, promoting LLPS at low concentrations via multivalent bridging and dissolving condensates at high concentrations via saturation, a switch recapitulated in cells and in mouse brain. These findings reframe HP1 condensation from an IDR-driven process to one cooperatively governed by IDR-folded domain interplay.

papers.title: Assembly and activation of the AAA+ motor of the multi-subunit cobaltochelatase
papers.abstract: Cobalamin is a complex yet essential cobalt-containing cofactor synthesized exclusively by prokaryotes and archaea. Aerobic cobalamin biosynthesis requires the CobNST multi-subunit class I cobaltochelatase for cobalt incorporation. Cobalt chelation is dependent on the energy transfer from the CobST AAA+/VWA motor unit to the substrate-binding catalytic unit (CobN). However, the mechanism for assembly and function of CobNST cobaltochelatase remains poorly understood. Here, we used cryo-EM to solve the structures of the AAA+ motor CobS, in the absence and presence of ATP and its VWA-partner protein CobT. Our data reveal that the AAA+ CobS assembles into various conformations, including hexameric planar rings and different spiral left-handed assemblies: hexamers, double rings and filaments. In the absence of nucleotide, the CobT N-terminal domain interacts with CobS left-handed oligomers, remaining in a half-assembled, nonfunctional motor unit. In the CobST complex, ATP induces conformational rearrangement of CobS from left-handed helical oligomers to a right-handed closed hexamer. The simultaneous repositioning of the CobT VWA domain to the AAA+ central pore shifts the motor unit to a functional state, ready-to-drive CobN-catalyzed chelation reaction. These findings define the mechanism for assembly and activation of the class I cobaltochelatase CobST motor.

papers.title: Pre-catalytic activation pathway of the Smc5/6 complex
papers.abstract: The Smc5/6 complex (Smc5/6) preserves genome stability through ATP-dependent DNA organization, but the structural details that prime the complex for productive DNA engagement remain unknown. Here, we combine cryo-electron microscopy and conformational heterogeneity analysis to define the pre-catalytic activation pathway of Smc5/6. We show that in the absence of ATP and DNA, Smc5/6 exists as a heterogeneous conformational ensemble composed predominantly of two conformations termed Bridge and Cross. In the presence of DNA alone, Smc5/6 adopts a Juxtaposed conformation that brings the ATPase heads into proximity, aligning them for nucleotide engagement. With both ATP and DNA associated, Smc5/6 establishes an Engaged architecture, within which DNA stabilizes its head-associated binding cavity through local remodeling of the complex. Conformational heterogeneity analyses suggest a continuous structural transition between the Cross and Juxtaposed states, while anisotropic network modeling identifies the Bridge-Cross-Juxtaposed-Engaged sequence as the mechanically favored pathway connecting the four experimentally observed conformations. Together, these findings support a pre-catalytic conformational pathway for Smc5/6 activation and provide a structural framework for understanding how conformational heterogeneity gives rise to an activation-competent motor state.

papers.title: Directed evolution of laccase from Thermus thermophilus HB27 reveals a variant with enhanced high temperature catalytic activity and electrochemical properties
papers.abstract: Laccases belong to the multicopper oxidase family (MCO). Compared with fungal laccases, bacterial laccases have high stability and activity under extreme pH and temperature conditions. Because of these characteristics, bacterial laccases have become highly impactful in industrial processes. In the present work, we engineered the Thermus thermophilus HB27 laccase (Tth-Lac) by directed evolution. The library had a size of 1.2 x105 colonies, and we screened mutants by malachite green decolorization on solid medium. The results showed that Q36H mutant exhibited higher catalytic activity than Tth-laccase (WT) at 90 degrees Celsius. Both enzymes showed similar pH profiles, but the activity at 90 degrees Celsius of Q36H mutant was X-fold higher than that of the wild-type enzyme. In contrast, the kinetic constants were similar for both enzymes. In the voltammetric responses, at 61.5 degrees Celsius, the Q36H mutant showed increased current, and the T1 copper potential shifted by 100 mV relative to the tth-Lac. These results suggest that the Q36H mutation has high potential for industrial applications because replacing a glutamine (Q) with a histidine (H) at position 36 enhances the enzyme's structural stability, allowing it to function efficiently under extreme temperature conditions.

papers.title: Inter-unit variability and rapid depletion of 2,3-diphosphoglycerate in stored red blood cells: implications for transfusion practice in neurocritical care
papers.abstract: Red blood cell (RBC) transfusion aims to restore tissue oxygen delivery, yet a stored unit's capacity to unload oxygen depends on 2,3-diphosphoglycerate (2,3-DPG), the principal allosteric modulator of hemoglobin-oxygen affinity. Randomized trials comparing fresher with older units have been consistently null, and all have used storage duration as the exposure variable. We asked whether storage age reflects the metabolic state of individual units. Twenty-four leukodepleted packed RBC units were sampled serially from day 3 to day 42 of standard cold storage. 2,3-DPG was quanti-fied by liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) with isotopically labelled internal standards, pH was measured in parallel, and trajectories were modelled by linear mixed effects with unit-level random intercepts. At day 3, 2,3-DPG spanned a twenty-fold range across units of identical age (0.8-14.7 mol/g Hb; median 4.8): some were already near-depleted at the earliest sampled timepoint, while others retained near-physiological concentrations. This heterogeneity collapsed rapidly - median val-ues fell to 27% of day-3 levels by day 7 and by more than 90% by day 14 ({beta} = -0.298 mol/g Hb per day, p < 0.001) - and were below the limit of detection in most units af-ter day 17. pH declined monotonically to 6.40 {+/-} 0.04 by day 42 ({beta} = -0.0163 units per day, p < 0.001). Units of identical storage age therefore differ markedly in the metabo-lite that governs oxygen unloading, and virtually all are depleted long before the 42-day expiry, indicating that storage-age dichotomies misclassify the exposure they are intended to represent.

papers.title: A Tandem Fluorescent Rh1::eGFP mCherry Reporter Reveals Rhodopsin 1 Trafficking and Turnover In Vivo in Drosophila Photoreceptors
papers.abstract: Rhodopsin 1 (Rh1), the major visual pigment of Drosophila photoreceptors, requires a vitamin A-derived chromophore for proper folding, maturation and transport to the rhabdomere. While the endocytic trafficking of mature, light-activated Rh1 to endolysosomal compartments is well characterized, the fate of immature Rh1 during defective ER maturation remains unclear. Here, we developed a Rh1::eGFP-mCherry tandem reporter to monitor Rh1 localization and compartment acidification in vivo. Exploiting the acid stability of mCherry, this reporter enables visualization of Rh1 after delivery to acidic environments and complements conventional antibody-based approaches. Under physiological conditions, pH-dependent quenching of eGFP fluorescence distinguished rhabdomeric Rh1 from Rh1 in acidic endolysosomal compartments. In vitamin A-deficient flies, immature apo-Rh1 accumulated within Calnexin-positive ER membranes, where we identified discrete acidified subdomains characterized by loss of eGFP fluorescence while mCherry fluorescence persisted. These structures remained continuous with the ER but were distinct from conventional endolysosomal compartments, revealing previously unrecognized acidified ER domains associated with immature Rh1. Together, our findings identify acidified ER subdomains as a previously unrecognized stage in Rh1 quality control and establish Rh1::eGFP-mCherry as a robust in vivo reporter for investigating rhodopsin trafficking, maturation and turnover under physiological and disease-relevant conditions.

papers.title: Triacylglycerol fatty acid composition modulates ATGL regioselectivity and diacylglycerol output
papers.abstract: Adipose triglyceride lipase (ATGL) catalyses the first and rate-limiting step of intracellular triacylglycerol (TAG) hydrolysis, yielding diacylglycerol (DAG) and a free fatty acid (FA). The site of TAG cleavage determines the regioisomeric identity of the DAG product, with distinct consequences for downstream signalling and lipid metabolism. Here, we show that ATGL prefers specific fatty acyl chain lengths and that this preference contributes to its regioselectivity on heterogeneous TAG substrates. Structural modelling identified a substrate-binding pocket comprising a hydrophilic anchor and a hydrophobic tunnel whose dimensions favour long-chain FAs. Mass spectrometry-based analysis of DAG products generated by ATGL from defined TAG substrates revealed an intrinsic preference for terminal (sn-1/sn-3) ester bond cleavage. Acyl-chain compatibility modulated this preference, with poorly accommodated terminal chains increasing the relative contribution of sn-2 cleavage. Consequently, ATGL generated predominantly sn-2-retaining DAG species from heterogeneous TAG substrates containing long-chain fatty acyl chains, including substantial amounts of the sn-1,2-DAG regioisomer, which has not previously been associated with ATGL activity. These findings link the fatty acyl chain composition of TAGs to the DAG regioisomer profile generated by ATGL-mediated lipolysis and provide substrate-dependent parameters for more species-resolved models of lipid metabolism.

papers.title: The role of a G-quadruplex structure in mediating the interactions of miR-1249-3p with the 3-UTR of the HNRNPK mRNA
papers.abstract: Heterogenous nuclear riboprotein K (hnRNP K) is an important regulator of multiple signaling pathways involved in DNA repair and function whose expression has been found to be mis-regulated in many cancers and neurological diseases. The expression regulation of hnRNP K is not fully understood however it has been shown that the microRNA miR-1249-3p targets its mRNA 3-untranslated region (UTR), regulating its translation. In this study we identified a guanosine-rich sequence in the HNRNPK 3-UTR within the miR-1249-3p binding site that has the potential to form a G-quadruplex (GQ) structure. By using various biophysical methods, we show that this sequence forms a parallel GQ structure which modulates the binding of miR-1249-3p to HNRNPK 3-UTR in vitro. Additionally, using luciferase reporter assays, we determined that this GQ structure affects the hnRNP K protein expression, suggesting modulation of the binding interaction of miR-1249-3p to the 3-UTR of HNRNPK. This HNRNPK mRNA GQ-miR binding axis is an unexplored mechanism of regulation, offering a novel therapeutic target for diseases caused by abnormal hnRNP K expression.
